en: *Abhiṣekaprakriyā* (The Procedure for Empowerment). Toh. no. 365. Derge Kanjur, vol.
KA, folios 146r.7–150r.7. Translated by Samantaśrī and Chos rab.
37 stanzas. Cf. Kaiser Library 139!!! 171\also–173\felso; 174\also–175\felso.
% 171\also–172\felso = 25 % 172\also–173\felso = 26 % 174\also–175\felso = 27
In the language of India: Śekhaprakriyā. In the language of Tibet: *Dbang gi rab tu byed pa* (The Treatise on Empowerment). Homage to the Great Compassionate One, the Noble Avalokiteśvara!
After the [deity] has been dismissed, one should perform protection for the head, heart, crown, navel, throat,
and secret place with the Victors residing in their respective families, using one's own three vajras.

Once the disciple has been given his body [anointment], dressed in yellow garments, and had his eyes covered, these vows—pertaining to the most excellent state—must be bestowed upon him here for the sake of concealment. (KCLT 3.92)
After having cast forth the *pravaragati*, [one should visualize it] at the head, the heart, the crown of the head, the navel, and the throat.
The Victors protect those born of their own lineage within the secrets that have abandoned the broad descent, by means of their own three vajras.
Having clothed the bodies of the disciples in yellow garments and covered their eyes, they should be led into this mandala.
For those who have proceeded upon the supreme path of conventional truth, their ascetic observances are to be given as constant offerings.

Abandon violence, untruth, another’s wife, another’s wealth, and likewise the drinking of intoxicants; these five are the noose of the thunderbolt in saṃsāra, the destruction of one’s own merit, and evil.

Whoever was at any time the teacher of gods and men, in his name this command of the Lord of the Universe— which destroys the fear of worldly existence— should be bestowed and likewise observed by you as well.
Having abandoned killing, untruth, and the wives of others, as well as the wealth of others and the drinking of intoxicants;
These five very sinful acts are the "Vajra Noose of Saṃsāra," which destroy one's own merit.
Whatever [gift] was bestowed by means of the name of whichever deity or human preceptor who appeared at that particular time;
By these words spoken by Viśveśvara, which destroy the fear of cyclic existence, you too must provide protection.
One should not engage in gambling, the consumption of blameworthy food, the recitation of wicked speech, the dharma of the spirits and lords of the Daityas,
or the fivefold slaughter of cows, children, women, men, and the Teacher of the Gods.

Betrayal of friends, lords, and the Teacher of gods and men, as well as those who trust in the Saṅgha; and the attachment of the senses—these are the twenty-five vows of the Lord of the World. (KCLT 3.94)
Attachment [to food, speech, and so forth], the Lord of the World, [and] the wearing of ornaments, as well as blameless food, the recitation of harsh words, and the dharmas of spirits and non-gods.
One must not kill the five venerable ones: oxen, children, women, men, and gods and humans.
One harbors resentment toward friends, masters, gods, human gurus, and the Saṅgha who provide consolation.
The senses are not possessed by attachment; these are the twenty-five observances of the Lord of Existence (Bhavabhartṛ).

Having consecrated it with the *śrī-mantra*, one flower should first be offered within the hollow of the cupped palms after being rotated three times; then, O King, the casting of the flower upon the mandala—
at whichever place that beautiful flower falls, that is certainly his [the practitioner's] family lineage.
Subsequently, the sevenfold initiation here is threefold, to be bestowed just as in the Unsurpassed [Tantra]. (KCLT 3.95)
KL: [Beginning] [25 recto] Here, the threefold consecration is to be bestowed just as the Unsurpassed [consecration].
Having offered a single flower into the joined lotus-palms of the glorious one who praises mantra, [25 verso] ... 146b6 ... joined together.
First, having circumambulated three times, one should cast the flowers held in the joined lotus-palms of the hands into the mandala.
O Lord of Men! Wherever a fine flower falls after the transformation of the basis, that very place is determined as its lineage.
Thereafter, the seven empowerments and the three [empowerments] shall be bestowed here exactly as they are, including the unsurpassed and perfect [empowerment].

O King, one should bathe the goddesses with four jars— whether made of jewels and gold or of clay— filled with gems, medicinal herbs, and perfumes, known as the *jaya* and *vijaya* jars, by means of the *nāgas*.
The excellent Guru bestows the crown with the various Buddhas and the headband with the Śaktis;
likewise, the vajra and bell [are bestowed], and the vow [should be understood] through the sun and moon, as well as by joining the sense objects with their corresponding faculties. (KCLT 3.96)
O King, with four *nāga* jars made of jewels and gold, or even of clay and containing gems,
filled with medicinal herbs and perfumes— the *Jayavijaya* jars— one should bathe the goddesses.
The excellent preceptor bestows the crown according to the various Buddhas, and the cloth [is bestowed] by means of the powers (*śakti*).
The vajra, the bell, the sun, and the moon, as well as the vow, should be joined with the sense objects and the sense faculties;
by the nāgas, together with the four [elements], and with the vase of the Victorious One, the All-Victorious (Vijaya), which is a gem or a golden vase.
Those born from that [lotus] shall be bathed by goddesses who possess jewels, medicinal herbs, and fragrances.
The supreme gurus, having donned the crowns of the various Buddhas, [adorned themselves] with silk streamers by means of the Śaktis.
With the vajra and bell, one should purify the objects and the sense faculties through the very practice of the sun and the moon.

While the Lords of Jinas, [manifesting] through loving-kindness and so forth, are not clearly perceived by those possessed of wrath, the command should be bestowed with equanimity. Having given the vajra and bell out of supreme compassion, one should teach the pure Dharma.
One should indeed commit the taking of life in the Vajra family; false speech in the Sword [family];
the theft of another's property in the Jewel [family]; and likewise, the taking of another's wife in the excellent Lotus family. (KCLT 3.97)
The Lord of Jinas has clearly given this command, equal in measure to the wrathful deities and the [four] immeasurables such as loving-kindness:

having bestowed the vajra and bell with supreme compassion, one should teach the pure Dharma. Indeed, one should commit the taking of life in the Vajra family, and likewise speak untruthful words in the Gaṅgā [Padma] family.
In the lineage of the noble lotus, even a jewel belonging to another must not be taken, nor should the wife of another be taken. (3)
By means of the names, he bestows the empowerments of the wrathful deities, the [deities] such as Maitreya, and the Lord of Victors, together with the outer permissions.
Having bestowed the vajra and the bell, one should teach the pure dharmas with supreme compassion.
For those certain to the Vajra family, one should engage in taking life and speak words of untruth with a sword.
In the *Ratnakula*, one should steal the wealth of others; in the supreme *Padmakula*, one should also abduct the wives of others.
Wine and lamps are the Buddhas, and all sense objects are to be enjoyed in the *Cakrakula*.
In the *Kartikākula*, the *ḍombī* and other women are to be served; in the *Khakula*, all women whatsoever are not to be despised.
For the sake of the welfare of sentient beings, you must give away this body along with its wealth; it is not to be preserved by you.
Otherwise, O son of noble family, Buddhahood will certainly not be attained even in infinite eons, as the Jina has declared. (KCLT 3.98)
O Cakra, wine, the continents, the Buddhas, and all the sense objects are to be enjoyed;
O Cakra, the Dombī and others, as well as all women, are to be taken in the hand of the *karttikā*, while other women are to be taken in the lotus of your mouth.
For the sake of the welfare of sentient beings, this body together with its wealth must be given away; it is not to be protected by you.
O son of noble family, Buddhahood does not indeed come about otherwise, even in infinite eons; so it has been spoken by the Jina.
In the maṇḍala, one should thoroughly cultivate the consumption of alcohol, lamps, the Buddhas, and all sensory objects.
In the *gri-gug* [mudrā], one should not disparage any woman whatsoever, such as a *caṇḍālī* and so forth, as being the lotus of space (*kha-yi padma*).
For the sake of sentient beings, you must give away both wealth and body; this is not something for you to protect.
O sons of noble family, the Victorious One has definitively taught that even in other countless eons, one does not become a Buddha otherwise.

The water is the goddesses beginning with Tārā; here, the Victors are the crown, the powers are the hero’s sash, and the vajra and bell are the sun and moon. The vow is also the objects [of the senses], namely the yoga of loving-kindness and so forth.
The command is the glory of perfect enlightenment, which crushes the fear of cyclic existence and is permeated by Kālacakra.
These seven empowerments, which remove the stains of defilement, are to be bestowed within the maṇḍala. (KCLT 3.99)
The water is the goddesses beginning with Tārā; the crown is the Victors; the hero’s sash is the Śaktis;
the vajra and bell are the sun and moon; the vow is the yoga of loving-kindness and so forth, known as the *vīkṣaṇā*;
the command is the Fortune of Perfect Awakening that crushes the fear of existence—these are conjoined with Kālacakra.
These seven consecrations, which remove the stains of defilement, should be bestowed within the mandala. || 4 ||
By means of water, [one worships] the goddesses such as Tārā; by means of the crown ornament, the Victors (Buddhas); and by means of the silk streamers, the Kanyās.
One purifies the vajra and bell, the sun and moon, the ascetic observances, the sense objects and so forth, and [the deities] such as Maitreya by means of their names.
The empowerment of the glorious Kālacakra, which pervades all time, overcomes the fears of existence, and brings about perfect enlightenment.
Thus, because the seven empowerments destroy the stains of sin, they are truly bestowed within the mandala itself.
Sprinkled with the seven consecrations, by the power of merit he attains sovereignty over the seven stages; furthermore,
having received the secret vase-consecration, he certainly enters the stage of non-retrogression and the rest.

One who has been consecrated with the wisdom-knowledge (prajñājñāna) attains the state of Mañjughoṣa, which crushes the fear of cyclic existence; yet, if through the influence of deceit one ever commits a root downfall, this leads to the suffering of hell. (KCLT 3.100)
One who has been sprinkled with the seven empowerments proceeds to the auspicious state and becomes a lord of the seven stages;
furthermore, one consecrated by the Vase and Secret empowerments certainly enters the stage of non-retrogression and so forth.
One consecrated by the Empowerment of Wisdom-Knowledge attains the state of Mañjughoṣa, who is venerated by the three worlds.
One may sometimes fall into a root downfall through the influence of deceit; this is the suffering of hell.
When the seven empowerments have conferred the empowerments, by the power of virtue, one becomes a sovereign of the seven stages.
Later, through the vase empowerment and the secret empowerment, one enters with certainty into the stages such as the irreversible [path].
By receiving the empowerments of wisdom and gnosis, one becomes Mañjughoṣa himself, who destroys the fears of cyclic existence.
If a root downfall occurs through the power of the world’s fickleness and deceit, even in this very life one will experience the suffering of hell.

For one who possesses the qualities, purification from a root downfall occurs when he abides in the sevenfold sprinkling; however, for one who has committed a root downfall, there is never purification through the secret vase or the higher [vases], even by virtue of vows and observances.
He who has fallen into a root downfall must enter this mandala again for the sake of purification.
For once he has received permission, he who was known as the eldest among the group of attendants again becomes insignificant. (KCLT 3.101)
Purification occurs for one who possesses [the required] qualities when established in the seven empowerments following a root downfall;
however, if it occurs in the Vase or Secret Empowerment, there is never purification through the power of vows and observances in the Higher Empowerment.
One who has committed a root downfall enters this mandala once again for the sake of purification.
For those who, having received the command, go again to the assembly of the Gaṇas, the one named Jyeṣṭha attains lightness.
If a root downfall occurs, one becomes completely purified by reciting [the mantra] while abiding in the seven empowerments and possessing virtuous qualities.
If there were no prior purification through the vase and secret initiations, which are the certain empowerments of ascetic discipline, [the higher ones would not exist].
Whoever has incurred a root downfall should enter this mandala for the purpose of purification.
If, after receiving the permission initiation (rjes gnang), one subsequently enters the class of the assembly, one is considered "younger" than those who are "elder."
A root downfall occurs for sons through causing mental distress to the glorious Guru;
another indeed occurs by transgressing his command, and likewise a third by anger toward one's brother.

Furthermore, the fourth [transgression] occurs from abandoning loving-kindness; the sixth from the loss of the thought of awakening; the seventh from reviling the established tenets; and the eighth for an unripened person from giving secret teachings. (KCLT 3.102)
A root downfall occurs for sons through the mental distress of the illustrious Guru;
another indeed occurs through transgressing his command, and likewise, the third through anger toward one's brother.

Furthermore, O Hero, the fourth [downfall] occurs through the abandonment of loving-kindness; the sixth through the destruction of the thought of awakening (*bodhicitta*); and also through disparaging the established tenets (*siddhānta*), or giving the secret even to an immature person. (6/8)
The root downfall is committed by the sons [disciples] when they have offended the mind of the glorious guru; it becomes the "Moon-holder" (the *candragraha* or *śaśadhara*).
To transgress his command is another [offense]; likewise, to be angry with one's own brother is certain to be the third.
By abandoning loving-kindness, one becomes the fourth; furthermore, from the total abandonment of the very mind of awakening, there is the arrow.
Furthermore, that very sixth disparagement of tenets is the bestowing of secrets upon people who have not yet reached maturity.
From the aggregates and afflictions there would be a snake; furthermore, the ninth is lack of interest in pure phenomena,
illusory loving-kindness, and conceptualization regarding that which bestows happiness devoid of name and so forth— this is Rudra.

Out of malice toward a pure being, even the Sun, when the time for giving has arrived, abandons her; indeed, among those established in the Vajrayāna, there arises a loathing for all other women. (KCLT 3.103)
From the aggregates and afflictions, there is a snake; furthermore, there is aversion toward the pure dharma as the ninth.
Then there is illusory compassion, and the conceptualization of name and so forth regarding that which bestows bliss—these directions are the Rudras.
Even the sun, through malice toward a pure being, may at times lose its light; likewise, for those established in the Vajrayāna, there is indeed a sense of revulsion toward all women. 9.
Through the afflictions of the aggregates, one becomes a nāga; furthermore, it is the ninth [cause]: lack of faith in the true Dharma.
Illusory love is intense conceptualization that bestows the bliss of being free from names and so forth.
To speak of the faults of pure beings will become like the sun; having abandoned the attainment of the samaya, it will be otherwise.
One who disparages any woman will certainly fall into a state of non-composure; this applies to those established in the Vajrayāna.
As long as ten years have passed since the beginning of the year, there is one [type of robe] which is of ten kinds, to be seen and touched.
Therefore, oceans full of nectar should be embraced and those beginning with *lā* (the *lādyāḥ*) should be served;
for mudrās over twenty years of age are extremely terrifying, being portions of wrathful spirits and asuras.
The six and four mudrās are for the purpose of consecration (*sekārtha*), bestowing the fruit of equal bliss; others are for the purpose of meditative cultivation (*bhāvanārtha*). (KCLT 3.118)

In the land of Kailāsa, until the age of ten, she is of one kind, to be seen and touched. Therefore, from [ten] up to twenty years, she is to be embraced; the oceans of nectar are to be served, as are the *lā* sounds and so forth. Beyond twenty years, the mudrās cause supreme fear, being portions of wrathful spirits and gods.
And thirty-six [deities] for the purpose of consecration (sekha), and others who bestow the fruit of equal bliss for the purpose of meditative cultivation (bhāvanā). || 10 ||
The regional years range from one up to ten, as they are both visible and tangible.
Then, the objects of embrace are the oceans, the flavorful things to be enjoyed, and the moving [objects] and so forth.
The mudrās of those under twenty years of age are the supremely terrifying wrathful bhūtas of the asura lineage.
Six and three [empowerments] are for the purpose of empowerment, bestowing the fruit of equal bliss; the others are for the purpose of meditation.

Even the first sprinkling on the jar-like breasts, which is to be touched by the glorious wisdom (*śrīprajñā*), is itself the secret-to-the-secret initiation (*guhyād guhyābhiṣeka*) through the tasting and gazing at the moon-holder (*śaśadhara*).

In the initiation of the wisdom-knowledge (*prajñājñāna-abhiṣeka*), having purified [the disciple] with all the Buddha-families through the limbs and faces, the consort (*mudrā*) should be given to the disciple by the Guru, having made even a Jina a witness in this matter. (KCLT 3.119) [Note: *śaśadharāsvādanālokābhyām* is adopted as the reading from manuscript S; *śaśadharāsvādanā lokanāḍyām* from manuscript B appears to be a corruption.]
The first touch of the glorious Wisdom [Buddha] here upon the breast is itself the pouring of water upon the jar;
through the tasting and embracing of the moon-holder (the tongue), it becomes the secret-to-secret initiation.

In the empowerment of the wisdom-knowledge (*prajñājñānābhiṣeka*), having purified [the disciple] with the limbs and faces belonging to all the Buddha-families, the Guru should bestow the consort upon the disciple, having made even a Jina a witness in this matter. (11)
That which first touches the breasts of the glorious Prajñā is itself designated as the vase empowerment.
By tasting the Holder of the Rabbit (the moon) and beholding the secret, one becomes fully established in the secret empowerment.
One should purify all the limbs and faces with the lineage of the Victors, and bestow the empowerment of the wisdom of insight.
Having acted as a heroic victor for the sake of his disciples, he bestows the mudrā; furthermore, here, [he does so] even for the guru.
Having desired with his own vajra-jewel, which consists of wisdom and means, a beautiful maiden of twelve years who is adorned with all ornaments, resembles molten gold, and is full of passion;
and having ascertained the purity of the disciple, he should cause even the vajra, together with its seed-syllable, to enter the disciple's mouth.
Thereafter, one's own mudrā should be given; then again, another [mudrā] endowed with the path of smoke and so forth.
Having made love with a beautiful maiden of twelve years, adorned with all ornaments and resembling molten gold,
who is impassioned, by means of his own vajra-jewel consisting of wisdom and method;
and having ascertained the purification of the disciple, he should cast his own seed— the vajra— into the disciple's mouth.
Afterwards, one's own mudrā should be offered; then again, another [mudrā] joined with the path of smoke and so forth. || 12 ||
A beautiful twelve-year-old girl, adorned with every ornament and resembling molten gold—such is the maiden herself.
For those possessed of passion, that which is to be enjoyed by means of one's own vajra-jewel is [attained] through being endowed with the nature of skillful means and wisdom.
Having recognized that the disciple is pure, one should indeed place the vajra seed-syllable into his mouth.
Later, having bestowed his own mudrā upon his son, he then [taught] the path of smoke and so forth to others as well.

O King, in the wisdom empowerment, these women must be avoided by a highly skilled preceptor: one who is terrified, distracted in mind, under the sway of a rogue, afflicted by disease, recently delivered, angry, rigid, fickle, addicted to lies and quarrels, physically deformed, or impure.
Those previously mentioned who are devoted to the Buddha and uphold the commitments of the guru are to be saluted and worshipped. (KCLT 3.121)

Those who are terrified, whose minds are bewildered, who are under the sway of the deceitful, afflicted by disease, or recently delivered; those who are angry, stubborn, greedy for wealth, addicted to falsehood and quarreling, or deficient in their own limbs due to impurity— [these are not to be honored].
O King, these [women] should be avoided by a very skillful master during the wisdom-consecration (*prajñābhiṣeka*);
however, those previously mentioned who are devoted to the Buddha and uphold the master’s commitments (*samaya*) are to be saluted and worshipped. 13.
A mind that is terrified, deluded, wavering, and under the sway of others, as well as one that possesses internal [afflictions] along with its offspring;
Angry, arrogant, attached to desire, delighting in contention, with impaired limbs and impure—148a4.
Thus, with great effort, the Guru should cause those who possess wisdom and gnosis to abandon that which is to be abandoned, O Lord of Men.
In response, he said: "One should prostrate to and make offerings to the Buddhas and Gurus, who possess devotion and uphold the samaya."

Sensual desire causes agitation in one's own mind; when it reaches fullness, that fullness becomes a flame which flows as a drop from the moon-bearing head after melting it. By nature, it provides excellent bliss through the upward suction of OṬṬĀ at the end of the three liberations of the drop.
This [experience] consists of attachment to the touch of light and the pleasure of emission, through the various stages of bliss (ānanda) and so forth. (KCLT 3.122)
Desires cause agitation in one's own mind; when fullness reaches its peak,
the full flame flows as a subtle drop from the head, having melted the moon-bearer.
By its very nature, it bestows excellent bliss through the emission of the *bindu* at the end of the three [stages];
then, this bliss of non-emission arises from the contact with light, through the distinctions of the various joys (*ānanda*) and so forth. (14)
The very minds of sentient beings are agitated and filled with passion.
From the blazing of that which fills the supreme limb, the Holder of the Moon melts and truly drips down.
By means of the excellent practice of summoning, the bindu that bestows supreme bliss reaches the end of the three liberations.
It is thus through the divisions of joy (*ānanda*) and so forth, consisting of appearance, contact, union, transformation, and bliss.

It produces the bliss of desire for men even at the very first by the sight with the eyes; later, during the occurrence of the full [bliss], it produces supreme bliss once again within one's own body.

The flame, dripping the drop, rejoices with the *viramānanda-vajra* in the lotus; at the end of the three drops, Oṭṭā brings about the innate bliss (*sahajānanda*)-vajra that has reached the unchanging state. (KCLT 3.123)
First, even at the mere touch of the lips, it produces the bliss of desire for men; later, during the full union, it produces supreme bliss once again within one's own body.
Then, as the flame flows down as a drop, she delights in the lotus by means of the vajra of the bliss of cessation (*viramānanda*).
At the end of the three drops of the *oḍā*, the emission [of the seed-syllable] produces the *bindu-vajra*. || 15 ||
At first, when all people behold her with their eyes, they are stirred by passion and filled with joy.
Thereafter, that which was full becomes perfectly gathered within one's own body, resulting in supreme bliss itself.
From the blazing of the fire, the drop (bindu) descends from the vajra into the lotus; this is the special joy (viramānanda).
In the *oḍḍā* vajra-activity, at the end of the three drops, bliss arises as the coemergent joy (*sahajānanda*).

The bliss of desire (*kāmānanda*) is accompanied by trembling and the syllable *ka*; that is the first union (*yoga*). Fullness (*pūrṇā*) and the arising of power (*śaktyudbhava*) indeed constitute the supreme bliss (*paramānanda*); this is the second.
Thus, the flame, the drop, and the *ghūrma*— and again the *viramānanda*— are likewise the third;
*ghūrma* [is read as] *mūrcchā* in manuscript B.
Oṭṭā, nāda, and nidrā, as well as sahajānanda—thus is the fourth.
The bliss of desire (*kāmānanda*), characterized by trembling and the syllable *Kampā*, is the first union through the fourfold [process].
The fullness (*pūrṇā*) is the arising of power (*śakti*), which is indeed the second, supreme bliss (*paramānanda*).
The flame (*jvālā*), the drop (*bindu*), and the dizziness (*ghūrmā*) are again the third, the bliss of cessation (*viramānanda*).
And *oḍā* is bliss (*ānanda*), and sleep is indeed the fourth, which is innate bliss (*sahajānanda*). || 16 ||
Through the four—desire, joy, movement, and immovability—there is its first application; fullness, capacity, birth, and certainty constitute the second, which is supreme joy itself.
The three [moments]—the ascending, the bindu, and the flowing—are indeed the third, the special joy (vishayānanda).
The *oḍḍā* and the mere sound itself, along with the innate joy (*sahajānanda*), constitute the fourth.
She is to be thought of as a mother by means of the mind; she becomes a sister through touching and embracing;
a daughter at the entry of the *vajra*; likewise, a niece during sexual union with its ritual application;
a wife at the falling of the drop; and a yoginī belonging to another family when passion has vanished.
These six yoga-mudrās consist of earth, water, fire, air, space, and cessation.

The mother is to be contemplated with the mind; the sister is for touching and embracing. The daughter is for the entry of the *vajra*; likewise, the sister’s daughter is for the son who possesses the ritual action (*sakaraṇa*).
The wife is for the falling of the drop (*bindu*); the yoginī from another family is for one whose passion has perished.
These six yoga-mudrās consist of earth, water, fire, air, space, and cessation. (17)
It is not to be contemplated with the mind; rather, it is to be touched and embraced, whereby she becomes a sister.
The vajra that has entered is called the daughter; likewise, the sister is that which possesses activity and is intensely blissful.
The falling of the *bindu* becomes minor; she is the Yoginī herself who belongs to another family, being free from passion.
Thus, the six mudrās of yoga are the entities that sever earth, water, fire, wind, and space.
In the lotus is the entry of the vajra, and in the fire is the falling of the drop; this third [stage] is the mudrā of body, speech, and mind, whose fixed nature is revealed by these three yogas.
The fourth is that which goes beyond passion and dispassion, a treasury of supreme qualities, accessible through yoga.
She is the mother of the mudrās, possessing tenfold aspects; she is the mouth of the illustrious Guru. (KCLT 3.126)
In the lotus [of the navel], there is the entry of the vajra; in the fire [of the heart], the falling of the drop (*bindu*) occurs through the wind, in due order.
These are the seals of body, speech, and mind, which are established as manifest for these three yogas.
The fourth, accessible through yoga, is the treasure-trove of supreme bliss, beginning with Rāga, Āra, Gāra, and Antaka.
She is the true mother of the *mudrās*, tenfold; she is the mouth of the glorious Guru. [Two circles]
When the vajra has entered the water-born [lotus], there is fire; then wind and the non-falling bindu follow in succession.
Thus, through the three yogas, the seals of body, speech, and mind are clearly and definitively established.
Attachment and detachment, the limit and the prior, and the treasure of supreme bliss—through application, this is the fourth armor.
That which is the supreme mother among the mudrās, possessing ten aspects, is this very face of the glorious guru.

Thus, according to worldly convention (*lokasaṃvṛti*), there are seven types of consecration (*abhiṣeka*). There are also three types and ten kinds; as for the fourth, it is stated again "likewise" (*tathā*). The supramundane consecration is the fourth, because of the statement that the fourth is not the third—the knowledge of wisdom (*prajñājñāna*)—but rather the fourth is the knowledge of wisdom, because of the statement "that again is likewise. Regarding this, the Blessed One said:

These ten—the seven aspects and the three aspects—are under the power of worldly convention (*saṃvṛti*), for it is said: "In that way, likewise, the fourth. The "fourth" is not the third, which is the wisdom-knowledge (*prajñājñāna*), because it is specified as the "supramundane fourth empowerment" (*lokottara caturtha-abhiṣeka*) and because it is stated "likewise. Here, the Blessed One declared:
"The touching of the seat of wisdom (*prajñāyā yā sthānasparśaḥ*), and the other, the embracing of the taste of the nectar (*amṛtāsvādana*)."

That which occurs during the fourth moment at the union with wisdom, when the bodhicitta has flowed and reached the state of nectar—all that is indeed mundane; yet, for the sake of the path, it is shown through supreme compassion.
The supramundane consecration is that which follows from the divine mudrā of the Supreme Victor.
The touching of the breasts through wisdom and means, and the embrace consisting of the tasting of another nectar;
that which occurs when the bodhicitta has melted and reached the state of nectar during the fourth moment upon union with wisdom.
All that is mundane has indeed been shown by the Supreme Compassionate One for the sake of the path;
that which is supramundane is the connection with the divine mudrās of the Supreme Lord of Victors.
That which is the very touching of the breast of wisdom, as well as the tasting and embracing of the nectar.
Through the union with wisdom, the bodhicitta itself melts and becomes nectar in four moments.
Supreme compassion has definitively taught that all of these have the mundane path as their cause.
He who follows the excellent seal of the sublime Lord of Victors, the transcendent power, 148b7.

Having abandoned this stained hearted *karmamudrā*, which is merely conceptualized, one should meditate upon the *divyamudrā*— the mother of the supreme Victors and the cause of perfect enlightenment—
as the *jñānamudrā*.

Untainted, changeless, as vast as space, all-pervading, accessible to yogins, immovable, possessing the splendor of gnosis, removing the impurities of existence, and permeated by Kālacakra. (KCLT 4.199)
Having abandoned this karma-mudrā, which is defiled in heart and merely imagined, [one should abandon] the jñāna-mudrās as well.
One should meditate on the divine mudrā, the mother of the supreme Victors, for the sake of perfect enlightenment.
Untainted, changeless, having destroyed both existence and non-existence, all-pervading, and attainable through yoga—
The *kūṭastha* [mudrā] is the splendor of gnosis, which removes the defilements of existence and is conjoined with the wheel of time;
for the *karmamudrā* is stained and distracts the mind, whereas the *jñānamudrā* consists of conceptualization.
Having truly abandoned [all else], the meditation on the excellent mudrā is that which gives birth to the Supreme Victor as the cause for perfect enlightenment.
Unstained, unchanging, dispelling darkness, all-pervading, and equal to space—this is that which is to be realized by the yogi.
The splendor of the primordial wisdom abiding in the body, which destroys the stains of existence, is pervaded by the wheel of time.

The mere appearance of the mind, produced within one's own consciousness like a reflection in a mirror, is indeed to be cultivated by the lords of yogis and practiced by all the sons of the Victors as well as by the Buddhas.
When that flame of wisdom has fully grown, it burns away the entire host of Māra together with its objects.
And by practicing for a year, they bestow passion and the rest upon their bodies, providing equal bliss to the excellent yogins.
The mere appearance of the mind, born from one's own intellect like a reflection in a mirror,
is indeed that which should be cultivated by the lords of yoga, who have [realized] all [phenomena].
It is the mere appearance of the mind, born from one's own intellect, certain to be like a reflection in a mirror.
When it has been practiced without exception by all the Sons of the Victorious Ones and the Buddhas, and cultivated by the lords of yogins, [it is the supreme path].
By the complete manifestation of that very light of primordial wisdom, the entire host of Māra, together with its domain, was incinerated.
Through the application of passion and the other [afflictions] to the body for one year, yogins bestow equal bliss.
Wisdom (*prajñā*), knowledge (*jñāna*), and mind (*citta*)— these constitute its tenfold appearance;
immersion (*majjana*) therein is indeed the consecration (*sekha*), which is like the reflection in a mirror resembling the stainless moon.

Therefore, that which is the bliss of nirvāṇa, the unchanging, the innate, and indeed the fourth— whosoever possesses this mouth of the Buddha situated in the heart and face, he is the glorious guru. (KCLT 5.114)
Regarding the phrase "wisdom-knowledge" (*prajñājñāna*): it is the very manifestation of the mind, and that [manifestation] becomes tenfold.
Whoever has entered this empowerment is certain to be like the reflection of the stainless moon in a mirror.
Then, one touches the fourth nirvāṇa—the unchanging coemergent bliss from which pleasure does not leak.
Therefore, he in whose heart and face the Buddha’s face resides is the glorious guru himself.
With minds unattached to space, with unblinking eyes, having entered the vajra-path, from emptiness there appear smoke, a mirage, a clearly manifest stainless firefly,
and a lamp; then flame, moon, sun, and vajras, as well as the supreme digit and the drop are seen.
In the midst of that, the form of the Buddha—the manifold *saṃbhogakāya* free from sense objects—[arises] like a flame, moon, and sun. (KCLT 5.115)
With the unblinking eye of the mind attached to space, those who have entered the vajra path—
From emptiness, smoke, mirages, and clear, stainless fireflies, and lamps [arise].
The fire, the sun, the moon, and the vajras, as well as others, are also the supreme parts and the bindus themselves.
In its center is the body of the Buddha, free from objects and conceptual constructs, consisting of manifold sambhogakāyas.
The yogi should gaze at the sky, free of clouds, with a steady vision,
until a black line, shimmering and pure-rayed, is seen within the channel of time (kālanāḍī).

Within that [wisdom], one's own mind—free from objects, possessing all colors and all forms, and unstained like the sun in water—is the image of the Omniscient One; it is not something other than mind itself. (KCLT 5.116)
That which is to be viewed with the view of one who abides in one-pointed yoga, appearing in a sky free from clouds, is as follows:
As long as one perceives the definitive black line emitting stainless rays of light, it is by means of the channel of time.

That omniscient body is stainless like the sun reflected in water, possessing manifold colors; it is the entirety of one's own mind, free from objects and conceptual forms, and is not the mind of another.
When the image has been seen, one should perform the restraint of the vital breath at every daily session until the wheel of rays, revolving and encircling one's own body,
is indeed perceived.
Within six months, the path-consciousness of practitioners— devoid of tactile sensation, equal in bliss,
and reaching the end of passion and dispassion— increases by the count of breaths for even a single moment of the Lord.
Having beheld the body, at each successive time of day and night, one should thoroughly arrest the very vital wind (*prāṇavāyu*).
For those possessing the ascetic observances, the mind on the path will, within six months, become free from tactile sensation and attain equal bliss.
Until one clearly perceives the light rays revolving completely like a wheel within one's own body.
From the first moment that one has gone to the extremes of attachment and detachment, the number of breaths of the pervasive lord increases.
Oḍrā is in the midst of the flames; Virama is between the innate (sahaja) and knowledge (jñāna); Vijñāna is in the middle [of them].
Nidrā is at the point of union (abhisandhi) of the whirlwind; that bliss which arises from the union of the pair (dvandvayoga) of the vajra and the lotus.
One should effect its increase through the power of the guru’s instructions; it increases, and there is nothing surprising in this.
Having slain the afflictions and the Māras, the excellent yogi enters the Lord of Jinas by means of the yoga of the year. (KCLT 5.118)
The limits, the center of the blazing, the special joy, the coemergent, primordial wisdom, and consciousness;
Whatever bliss arises from the union of the vajra and the lotus abiding in the midst of sleep and fainting, [that is the supreme bliss].
Through this, one should cause [the practice] to increase; by the power of the Guru’s certainty, there is no doubt that this very [practice] will increase.
By practicing for one year, the yogin dwells as a sovereign victor who conquers Māras and the afflictions.

It has the form of earth, yet it is firm and not of the nature of flowing water; it is not liquid because it lacks fluidity, yet it is not fire because it has the form of fire; it is not air because it is motionless, though its body is like the moving wind;
it has the form of emptiness, yet it is visible; it possesses white, green, and all the great colors of the universe, yet it is not a color.
Even though he possesses all forms, he remains invisible due to the power of the Māra of the afflictions, which turbidly defiles his own heart. (KCLT 5.119)
Although it appears as Vairocana, it is not solid; and although it appears in the form of water, it is not water, because it lacks moisture.
Though it appears as fire, it is not fire; though it appears in the form of wind, it is not wind because it is without movement.
Although it is of the nature of emptiness, it is seen; though white, blue, and so forth are seen, they are not manifold colors.
Although it possesses all aspects, one does not see it due to the stains of one's own mind, the afflictions, and the power of Māra.

Nāda, bindu, kalā, and knowledge—these reside in the state of immortality; the channels are bound together like a chain, with the three paths of prāṇa and apāna; the vajra is joined with the lotus, and likewise the lotus is joined with the vajra.
In the midst of the collision of the two winds, there is the exit and entry of the objects and the subjects;
furthermore, the grasping of the signs such as smoke—all this is the secret. (KCLT 5.120)
The mere sounds, the drops (bindu), the parts, and the primordial wisdoms proceed to the abode of nectar; they are the channels bound by iron chains.
Through the three channels of prāṇa and apāna, together with the vajra-lotus and the lotus-vajra.
In the center, the movement and entry of the winds are perfectly gathered, becoming free from object and subject.
The signs such as smoke and so forth, as well as all that is apprehended and these very apprehenders, are the great secret.
The entry of the vital breath into the center, the binding of the movements of the sun and moon in the right and left channels,
the mind reaching supreme bliss through union with the mudrā, and the awakening of the vajra;
or the sound of the vajra in the lotus, or the splashing of water from one's own hands for the sake of pleasure.
The abandonment of the seed-syllables, accompanied by bliss and removing the fear of death—this is the mouth of the venerable Guru. (KCLT 5.121)
The insertion of the life-force in the center consists of binding the right and left [channels], which have become the sun and moon respectively.
Through union with the mudrā, the mind attains supreme bliss, and the vajra is perfectly awakened.
For the sake of supreme bliss, one should stir the vajra within the lotus, or rotate it with the lotus of one’s own hand.
That bliss, in which no seed has been sown, is the very face of the glorious guru, which overcomes the fear of death.

Earth dissolves into water, and water likewise into fire; fire into wind, and wind into space; and space indeed proceeds into the tenfold causal sign, and the causal sign into the Jñānakāya, which is unstruck, supreme bliss, imperishable, and endowed with all aspects.
O Lord of Men, through knowledge, supernatural power and spiritual accomplishment arise for men in this very life. (KCLT 5.122)
That enters into water, and water likewise into fire; fire, in turn, enters into wind.
The wind is within emptiness; emptiness becomes the ten kinds of signs, endowed with all aspects of signs.
Possessing all aspects, it becomes the supreme, indestructible bliss, the body of gnosis (*jñānakāya*).
From wisdom, O Lord of Men, the siddhi of miraculous powers arises; for men, in this very life.
Desire arises as the emanation body (nirmāṇakāya); his speech alone is certainly complete;
the flame is the emanation mind that produces supreme bliss; and his wrath is indeed gnosis itself.
Ānanda is the enjoyment body (*bhogakāya*); through this sequence, it becomes the supreme *viramānanda*.
Indeed, the speech and mind of this Śambhu become the gnosis-vajra (*jñānavajra*), which is precisely his innate joy (*sahajānanda*). (KCLT 5.123)
Through desire, one will certainly become the nirmāṇakāya; through fullness, one will become the supreme vākkāya.
The mind of the emanation of the intermediate state is expressed as the wisdom that brings about supreme bliss from the syllable OḌḌĀ.
Joy is the saṃbhogakāya, the supreme; through the sequence of [joy] together with special joy and so forth.
From speech and mind—namely, coemergent joy and so forth—the Vajra of Gnosis and the others arise.
Kampā is indeed the Dharmakāya, saluted by the three worlds; from it arises Vāg, which is Ghūrmā.
Dharmacitta is indeed the destruction of the fear of existence, and its sleep is Jñāna.
Varṇa is indeed the Śuddhakāya; the vowels, devoid of *kalā*, *bindu*, and *nāda*, follow in sequence.
Speech and mind are the gnosis-vajra, existing within the threefold existence; they belong to Śambhu, whose body is pure. (KCLT 5.124)
The moving one is certainly the Dharmakāya; it is that which is honored by the three worlds and from which its speech arises.
Sleep is certainly the heart of the Dharma; that *turya* is itself primordial wisdom, which destroys the fear of cyclic existence.
The body of definitive purity of syllables, through the stages of the portion devoid of vowels and the mere sound of the bindu.
The vajras of speech, mind, and primordial wisdom purify the three realms of existence and generate them as the pure bodies.
Furthermore, this other [state], which has the nature of waking and dreaming, and the essence of deep sleep and the fourth state (turya),
moves through objects while remaining within the body, absorbed in the breath; it moves while the mind is absorbed and motionless.

If one who abides in gnosis should, through attachment to women, have the thought of awakening (bodhicitta) melt for even a moment, then the Mind-Vajra will certainly arise in its fourfold form through the sequence beginning with the Emanation Body. (KCLT 5.125)
The nature of waking and dreaming, as well as that of deep sleep and the fourth state (turya), are likewise [of the same nature].
The body remains still, the breath itself dissolves, the mind flows without movement, and the mind dissolves from its objects.
Even while abiding in primordial wisdom, at the very moment the bodhicitta melts through intense union with a woman, //
Through the sequence beginning with emanation and so forth, the fourfold vajra of mind is definitively established.

Thus, the mind— fourfold and residing within the three types of existence— is to be protected by the lords of yogis within the *bindu* of living beings; it bestows the fruit of equal bliss, is all-pervasive, and serves as the cause for liberation.
If there is liberation upon the release of a drop, where then is liberation for yogins whose seed of birth has attained supreme bliss?
Therefore, this momentary pleasure of saṃsāra must always be avoided here by ascetics. (KCLT 5.126)
Thus, within the bindu of the three types of existence of sentient beings, the mind exists in four ways; [it is] to be abandoned.
The lords of yogins should protect that which bestows the fruit of pervasive, equal bliss as the cause of liberation. 150a6. To be protected: //
If the seed-drop (bindu) is emitted to produce supreme bliss for yogins, how could liberation ever occur?
Therefore, those who have taken up ascetic vows should constantly abandon this momentary pleasure of saṃsāra.

[*ūṃ āḥ hūṃ hoḥ] First, one should always awaken [the wine] here by those situated in the sequence; having purified it and ignited it, one should contemplate it gradually, like the molten moon.

Taking a drop from that vessel with the tip of the ring finger of the hand that resembles the moon's rays, one should draw a triangle resembling the sun on the ground outside, and a circle in its center.

Having meditated upon that wheel of gnosis in the center, which has pervaded even the three realms of existence, that mantra-practitioner performs the libation and other rites daily with the thumb and ring finger.

First, the mantra practitioner should offer a bali-oblation here to the lords of regions and villages using their names at the beginning, middle, and end; furthermore, two morsels for Hārītī and a bali-oblation for the King of Wrath.
The Vajra-husbands give the foremost portion of the food to the female messengers (dūtīs) while they reside upon the surface of the earth;
then, they recite this auspicious verse of giving regarding the remains of what has been eaten by the spirits (bhūtas).

One should perform the *aṅganyāsa* with one's own vajras on the head, throat, heart, navel, secret place, and crown; likewise during sleep, in worship, and in sexual union, using the limbs and faces belonging to both families. || O ||
Homage to the glorious Kālacakra!
Oṃ hrāṃ, homage to the heart (maḥ).
Oṃ hrīṃ, svāhā to the head. Oṃ hūṃ, vauṣaṭ to the crest-lock.
Oṃ hūṃ, for the armor, hūṃ. Oṃ hūṃ, for the eyes, vaṣaṭ. Oṃ hraḥ, for the weapon, phaṭ.

Now, regarding the fourth [joy] in the ultimate truth, it is likewise as follows: that which was spoken by the Blessed One is the fourth joy, the outflow (*niḥsyanda*) of that [wisdom]. This is because of the statement "the fourth," and because of the statement "it is likewise as follows. That very thing is the wisdom of gnosis (*prajñājñāna*), yet it is devoid of the action-seal (*karmamudrā*) and the gnosis-seal (*jñānamudrā*). This is because its intrinsic nature is the joy that is the outflow of that [wisdom], and because it is produced from the gnosis of the great seal (*mahāmudrā*). It does not constitute the knowledge of the action-seal or the gnosis-seal. And regarding this, the Blessed One said:

"He possesses all forms yet is formless; he holds the sixteen [digits], the half-bindu, and is partless, transcending calculation, holding the pinnacle of the fourth dhyāna"—thus it is read in the *Nāmasaṃgīti*. This Blessed One does not "hold a drop" (*bindudhṛk*) in the manner of other ordinary beings. Rather, he holds the fourth pinnacle among the dhyānas of bliss (*ānanda*), supreme bliss (*paramānanda*), the cessation of bliss (*virama*), and the innate bliss (*sahaja*). He does not "emit" (*sṛk*), because he is without passion (*avirāga*).
The cause is all-aspected yet formless; it is wisdom (*prajñā*), and its fruit is the method (*upāya*) consisting of sixteen, eight, four, and two drops (*bindu*). Thus the Blessed One has said:
"One should observe the mind within the jewel from the vajra-posture;
until it reaches stainlessness, it is filled with the bliss of the natural outflow (*niḥsyanda*) and so forth."

At the navel, it is said to be the state of outflow (*niḥsyanda*); at the heart, it is known as maturation (*vipāka*); at the throat, it is human effort (*puruṣakāra*); and at the head of the Lord, it is purity (*vaimalya*).

Therefore, the bliss of emission (*virāma*) in the external [body] does not bestow Buddhahood, because it is established in both cyclic existence (*bhava*) and nirvāṇa. The knowledge of the Blessed One, however, is non-abiding in both cyclic existence and nirvāṇa, because it is infallible (*acyuta*). Cyclic existence is the place of birth at the forehead; nirvāṇa is the vajra-union of the four drops.
[164] Also, a folio 31 of a *Kālacakra* exegetical work [retraced? not the same hand!]. [31 recto] ...
thus it is established. That which is unestablished extends from the forehead to the *vajramaṇi*; externally, it is blood. And so the Blessed One has said:
Without beginning or end, peaceful, the exhaustion of existence and non-existence, all-pervading,
and inseparable from emptiness and compassion— this is known as bodhicitta.

"Without beginning or end, free from arising and decay. "Peaceful," meaning free from the fluctuations of the sense faculties. "The exhaustion of existence and non-existence," meaning free from eternalism and nihilism. "The Lord of the three realms of the earth. "Inseparable from emptiness and compassion": emptiness is liberation at the tip of the vajra; compassion is existence at the forehead. Between these two is non-dual gnosis; this is remembered as the Blessed One’s *acyuta-sahaja* (the innate that is non-emitted). This is stated in the *Ḍākinīvajrapañjara*: "The first is the vase initiation; the second is called the secret."
But the third is the gnosis of wisdom (prajñājñāna), which... [is that which...]
As it is not so, thus is the Tathāgata;
[this is] a quotation from the *Ḍākinīvajrapañjara* in the *Tathādibuddha*.
Having abandoned the action-seal (karmamudrā) and the conceptualized wisdom-seal (jñānamudrā),
one should practice the great seal (mahāmudrā) through the yoga of the supreme unchanging (paramākṣara).
Thus, from the supramundane consecration... [the 11th consecration] ...to the glorious Kālacakra. Oṃ āḥ hūṃ hoḥ haṃ kṣaḥ. Thus are the wheels. Purification by means of the syllable Oṃ.
Awakening by means of the syllable ĀḤ;
igniting (or kindling) by means of the syllable HŪṂ;
and transforming into nectar by means of the syllable HOḤ.
Invocation is performed with the syllable *haṃ*;
dismissal with the syllable *kṣaḥ*.
Therein, one should purify with the left hand.
One should awaken [it] with the right hand;
having joined the palms together, one should kindle [it];
and by means of the Garuḍa-mudrā, one should make it nectar (*amṛta*).
One should summon with the vajra-mudrā;
one should dismiss with the back of the hand.

Having meditated on the liquor as having the nature of the flowing moon, one should then take a drop of that liquor from the vessel with the ring finger of the left hand and draw a triangle, the *dharmodaya*, upon the ground. In its center, one should draw a circle in the form of a drop (*bindu*). One should contemplate the wisdom-maṇḍala like a reflection in a mirror. One should perform its libation with clear [liquor], using the following words: *Oṃ āḥ hūṃ hoḥ kāyavākcittajñānavajriṇi*. Then: *a ā i ī ṛ ṝ u ū ḷ ḹ*—these are the aggregates beginning with consciousness and the elements beginning with space. *a ā e ai ar ār o au al āl ha hā ya yā ra rā va vā la lā ṇa ṇā*—these are the six sense faculties and the objects of the senses such as sound, etc. *ha hā ya yā ra rā va vā ṇa ṇā*—these are the ten wrathful deities whose nature is method and wisdom.

The nature of the sense faculties of karma, such as Dveṣavajrī and the others: ka kā, kha khā, ga gā, gha ghā, ṅa ṅā; ca cā, cha chā, ja jā, jha jhā, ña ñā; ṭa ṭā, ṭha ṭhā, ḍa ḍā, ḍha ḍhā, ṇa ṇā; pa pā, pha phā, ba bā, bha bhā, ma mā; ta tā, tha thā, da dā, dha dhā, na nā; sa sā, śa śā, ṣa ṣā, ska skā, ha hā; ya yā, ra rā, va vā, la lā; kṣa kṣā.
